The Cuban Missile Crisis was a thirteen-day confrontation between the Soviet Union and the United States (US) during the Cold War, triggered by the US discovery of missile deployments on Cuba, an island country located just 90 miles off the coast of Florida, USA. The crisis is often regarded as the closest the world has come to a nuclear war.

In October 1962, US President John F. Kennedy learned about Soviet ballistic missiles being installed in Cuba through U-2 spy plane photographs. This revelation led to an intense standoff between the two superpowers and sparked international concern as these missiles threatened the security of the United States.

The crisis ended on October 28, 1962, when Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev agreed to remove the missiles in exchange for a US and NATO promise not to invade Cuba and to remove US Jupiter missiles from Turkey (a key strategic location for the United States). This event marked a significant turning point during the Cold War and demonstrated the potential catastrophic consequences of nuclear proliferation.
